narrative:
The model has analyzed your academic situation and determined that there’s a **12% chance** you might not pass your final year. While this might seem low, the school has set a threshold of **10%**—meaning any student with even a small risk of struggling is required to take extra support courses to help them succeed.

The decision isn’t random—it’s based on three key factors that stood out in your profile. The most important was your **past academic performance**, which shows you haven’t had any previous failures. While this might seem like a positive, the model actually sees it as a **warning sign**. Most students who pass don’t have a history of failing classes, so your lack of failures suggests you might not have faced enough academic challenges yet. Without this experience, you may be less prepared for the demands of your final year.

The second factor is your **long-term goals**. You’ve said you want to pursue higher education, which is great—but the model notes that many students who aim for university often push themselves harder, while others who don’t plan ahead may struggle more. Since you *do* have these goals, this actually works in your favor, slightly reducing the risk.

The third factor is whether you’re getting **extra educational support**. Right now, you’re not receiving any additional help from the school, unlike most students who pass. Since your final year is critical, the school wants to make sure you have the resources you need to succeed.

To improve your chances, focus on **balancing your study time**—most successful students dedicate **5 to 10 hours a week** to their coursework. Since you’re currently studying **only 2 to 5 hours**, increasing this could make a big difference. Also, while your family relationships are strong, the model suggests that students who get **family support** for their studies tend to do better. Finally, since you haven’t had failures before, this is a good time to **proactively seek help** if you ever feel overwhelmed—it’s better to address small challenges now than face bigger ones later.

The remedial courses aren’t a punishment—they’re a chance to build the habits and support system you’ll need to pass confidently.
